encodingDesc.p: Two supplied OCR witnesses of George W. Mooney (1930), Indiana (INU) and Pennsylvania State (PST). INU is the base; selected clearer PST readings and all witness disagreements are recorded in the accompanying audit. Source wording, including unresolved OCR and editorial differences from Ihm, is retained. This is an OCR draft, not a proofread transcription. Chapter/section references align with Ihm (perseus-lat2). English inner-section boundaries are editorial and have been reviewed against corresponding clauses; printed chapter boundaries are retained. No translation is supplied from Rolfe or Gemini. Commentary section signs are preserved (including OCR $ for §). Domitian 13.3 is aligned by the consulatus septemdecim lemma where the sign is absent. Lemmas use mentioned linked to note type=commentary, following the Sidgwick model. Literal bibl references and explicit glosses are marked without invented reference expansions. Unconfirmed note openings and OCR reading-order issues remain in the review inventory. Introductory material, appendices and index remain available in the complete source-page archives; they are not included in these life-specific reading texts.

div.p: Titus, of the same surname as his father, was the darling and delight of mankind; such an abundance had he of natural gifts, or of adroitness, or of good luck, to win for him the affections of all, and that, too, which is most difficult, while he was emperor; for as a private citizen, and even during his father's reign, he did not escape hatred, much less public censure. He was born on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the year remarkable for the murder of Gaius, near the Septizonium, in a mean house and in a very small and gloomy room; for it is there as a show-place to this day.

He was brought up at court along with Britannicus, trained in the same subjects and by the same teachers. During this time, as they tell, a brow-reader was brought in by Narcissus, the freedman of Claudius, to examine Britannicus, and affirmed most positively that under no circumstances would he ever become emperor, whereas Titus, who was standing beside him, assuredly would. The two were such close friends, that it is believed that Titus, who was reclining at table beside him, also tasted of the deadly potion which Britannicus drained, and thus was stricken by a grievous sickness for a long time after. Mindful of all this in later days Titus set up a golden statue to Britannicus in the Palace, and dedicated to him another of ivory, an equestrian statue, and attended it in the Circus-processions, at the head of which it is borne to the present day.

Even in boyhood his endowments both of body and of mind shone forth, and more and more so in each successive stage of life: a striking figure, blending grace and majesty alike; exceptional strength, although he was not tall of stature and his belly protruded rather much; a wonderful memory ; an aptitude for almost all the arts both of war and peace.

He was unsurpassed for skill in arms and horsemanship. He used both the Latin and Greek tongues, whether for oratory or the fashioning of verses, with such readiness and ease, that he could even improvise. Neither was he a stranger to music, as he both sang and played with charm and taste. Many persons have told me that he used also to take down in shorthand with the greatest speed, competing for sport and fun with his own secretaries, and that he could imitate any handwriting that he had ever seen, often declaring that he might have been a master forger.

He served as military tribune both in Germany and in Britain, winning the highest commendation for his energy and not less for his probity, as is clearly shown by the multitude of statues and busts with inscriptions to him in either province.

After serving in the army he applied himself to pleading in the Forum, seeking fame more than a steady practice. At the same time he took as wife Arrecina Tertulla, whose father was indeed only a Roman knight, but had been prefect of the praetorian cohorts; on her death he filled her place by Marcia Furnilla, of a most illustrious house, but divorced her after she had borne him a daughter whom he acknowledged as his own.

Then, having held the office of quaestor, he was given command of a legion and he reduced to subjection Taricheae and Gamala, two of the strongest cities in Judaea, having his horse killed under him in one engagement and mounting another, whose rider had fallen fighting by his side.

Soon afterwards, when Galba came into possession of the State, he was sent to congratulate him, and wherever he went he turned the eyes of all upon him, from a belief that he had been sent for to be adopted. But when he perceived that everything was once more in confusion, he turned back from his journey and visited the oracle of the Paphian Venus, where, while he asked counsel about his voyage, he was at the same time confirmed in his hope of empire.

Soon he saw his hope a certainty, and being left behind to complete the subjugation of Judaea, at the final assault on Jerusalem he slew twelve of its defenders with as many arrows, and took the city on his daughter's birthday, so delighting and captivating the soldiers that in their congratulations they all saluted him as Imperator; and soon after, when he was for leaving the province, they tried to hold him back, demanding with entreaties, nay, even with threats, that he should either remain or take them all with him.

This bred a suspicion that he was trying to revolt from his father and to claim for himself the sovereignty of the East; and he strengthened this suspicion when, on his way to Alexandria, he wore a diadem at the consecration of the bull Apis in Memphis, which he did in accordance with the custom and ritual of that old religion, but there were not wanting some who interpreted it amiss. Wherefore he hastened to Italy, and having put in at Regium and then at Puteoli in a transport vessel, he went with all speed from there to Rome, and taking his father by surprise he said, as if to prove how ill-founded the rumours about him were, "Here I am, father, here I am!”

From that time on he never ceased to play the part of sharer and even protector of the empire. He triumphed with his father, and held the censorship together with him; further he was his colleague in the tribunician power and in seven consulships. He took upon himself the duties of almost every office; for in his father's name he dictated letters, drafted edicts, and even read his father's speeches in the senate in place of the quaestor. He also assumed the prefectship of the praetorian guards, which hitherto had never been held by any but a Roman knight. In this position he acted in a decidedly arrogant and despotic fashion; for whenever any had aroused his private suspicions very strongly, he first sent secret emissaries into the theatres and
camps to demand their punishment as if by general consent, and then without scruple put them to death.

Among these was Aulus Caecina, a man of consular rank, whom he invited to dinner and then ordered to be stabbed almost before he had left the dining-room; in his case, admittedly, urged by a pressing danger, for he had found in the handwriting of Caecina a speech which he had prepared to deliver to the soldiers. By such deeds, though he provided for his future safety, he incurred intense odium at the time; so that it would be hard to find anyone who came to the throne with such an evil reputation and amid such general disapproval.

Besides his cruelty he was also suspected of luxurious living, because he prolonged till midnight his drinking-revels with the most prodigal of his boon-companions; likewise of lewdness, by reason of his troops of profligates and eunuchs, and by reason of his notorious passion for queen Berenice, to whom, as report went, he even promised marriage. Moreover he was suspected of graspingness, because it was well known that in cases which came before his father he used to make bargains and accept bribes for his influence. In short, people both thought and said openly that he would prove a second Nero. But this reputation turned out to his advantage and changed to the most unbounded praise, when no vice was found in him, but on the contrary the highest virtues.

The banquets which he gave were enjoyable rather than extravagant. He chose for his friends men in whom the succeeding emperors also reposed confidence as indispensable to themselves and to the State, and whom they employed above all others. Without delay he sent Berenice away from the city, against her will and against his own. Some of his most favoured minions, though so skilled in dancing that soon they completely dominated the stage, he not only refrained from pampering unduly, but even from witnessing any performance of theirs at a public concourse.

He took away nothing from any citizen; he kept his hands from others' property, if any man ever did; he would not accept even the allowable and customary contributions. And yet he did not fall short of any of his predecessors in munificence. On the occasion of the dedication of his amphitheatre and the rapid completion of the adjoining baths he gave a spectacle most sumptuously appointed and on the most lavish scale; he also exhibited a naval battle in the old Naumachia, and gladiators in the same place, and five thousand wild beasts of all kinds in a single day.

He had a most kindly nature, and though in accordance with the precedent established by Tiberius all the succeeding Caesars had refused to ratify privileges granted by their predecessors, unless they themselves had granted the same privileges to the same people, Titus was the first to confirm by one single edict all past favours, without waiting to be asked. In dealing with other requests of his subjects he adhered inflexibly to the principle of sending no one away devoid of hope. Nay more, when the stewards of his household reminded him that he was promising more than he could perform, he replied: "None should ever go away sad at heart from an interview with his emperor." Further, when on one occasion he recalled at dinner that he had bestowed nothing on anyone during the entire day, he gave utterance to that memorable and justly praised saying: "Friends, I have lost a day."

The masses especially he treated with such graciousness on all occasions, that when he announced a gladiatorial spectacle, he declared that he would give it in accordance with the wishes of the spectators, and not his own; and this was precisely what he did. For he refused not any request of theirs, and even urged them to ask for anything they liked. Nay more, he openly showed his preference for gladiators armed in Thracian fashion, and often both with words and gestures indulged in lively interchanges with the spectators, like a regular partizan, but without any sacrifice of dignity or fairness. To neglect no means of winning favour, at times he admitted the lower orders to his new-built baths when he himself was bathing there.

Some deplorable disasters happened in his reign, such as the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Campania, a fire which raged at Rome for three whole days and nights, and a dire plague not easily paralleled. In calamities of such magnitude he displayed not merely the concern of an emperor, but even a father's matchless love, now by offering consolation through his edicts, now by giving succour as far as his means allowed.

He appointed commissioners by lot from among the ex-consuls for the restoration of Campania; and the property of those who had been overwhelmed by Vesuvius and had no heirs forthcoming he devoted to the reconstruction of the devastated cities. During the fire in the capital the only public pronouncement that he made was "I am ruined," and he set apart all the ornaments of his country palaces for the new buildings and temples, and put over the work many men of equestrian rank, that everything might be completed the more quickly. For curing the sickness and alleviating the disorders there was no aid, divine or human, which he did not employ, searching out every form of sacrifice and healing.

Among the evils of the times were the informers and their prompters, by reason of the long licence which they had enjoyed. After these had been soundly beaten with scourges and cudgels in the Forum, and finally led in mockery through the arena of the amphitheatre, he ordered some of them to be put up and sold as slaves, and some to be transported to the most rugged islands. And to check for ever those who at some future date might venture on like practices, he, among other restrictions, forbade the bringing of actions on the same matter under more laws than one, and the inquiring into the legal status of a deceased person after a specified number of years.

Having declared that he accepted the office of chief pontiff in order to keep his hands unstained, he made good his word; for from that day he was neither the cause of, nor privy to, the death of any, though at times he lacked not grounds for vengeance; but he swore that he would rather be slain than slay. When two men of patrician stock were convicted of aspiring to the empire, he did nothing more than warn them to desist, pointing out that empire was a gift of Fate, and promising that he would give them whatever else they might desire.

And straightway he despatched his own couriers to the mother of one of them, for she was at a distance, to inform the anxious lady that her son was safe; as to themselves, he not only invited them to a dinner of his particular friends, but on the following day at a gladiatorial spectacle he designedly placed them close to him, and when the swords of the combatants were offered to him, he tendered them for their inspection. It is said, moreover, that he ascertained the horoscope of each of them, and assured them that a danger overhung them both, but at some future date and from another, as proved to be the case.

Though his brother never ceased scheming against him, but alnost openly tampered with the armies and plotted flight to them, he could not bear to put him to death or remove him from Rome, or even to hold him in less honour; but, as he had ever done from the first day of his reign, he persistently avowed that he was his partner and successor, and at times in private he implored him with prayers and tears to bring himself even now to return his affection.

In the midst of all this he was cut off by death, more to the loss of mankind than to his own. After he had finished the public spectacles, at the close of which he had shed abundant tears in presence of the people, he set out for his Sabine estate, somewhat cast down because a victim had escaped while he was making sacrifice, and because thunder-peals had been heard in a cloudless sky. Then at the very first station on the road he got a fever, and as he was being removed thence in a litter, it is said that he drew back the curtains and looked up to heaven, complaining bitterly that his life was being snatched away from him quite undeservedly; for there was no action of his of which he had reason to repent, except one, and one only.

What that was, he neither revealed himself, nor could one readily divine. Some think that he was calling to mind the intimacy which he had once enjoyed with his brother's wife; but Domitia most solemnly swore that none such had existed, though she was not the woman to deny it, had there been any truth in it; nay, she would certainly have boasted of it, as she was ever ready to do of all her deeds of shame.

He died in the same country-house as his father, on the Ides of September, two years two months and twenty days after he had succeeded his father, and in the forty-second year of his age. When his death became known, the whole people mourned as in some family bereavement; the senate rushed to the senate-house before they were called together by proclamation and while the doors were still shut; afterwards, when the doors were opened, they rendered him such thanks and heaped such praise upon him, now that he was dead, as they had never done before even while he was still alive and present among them.
